trails.bestSeason: Year-round; best Oct-Apr to avoid summer heat
trails.trailTip: The pavement has uneven, sometimes loose-gravel sections on the descent into the badlands, so sturdy shoes help even on this short loop.
trails.didYouKnow: Blue Mesa's blue-gray hills are bentonite clay that swells and shifts with every rain, slowly exposing new petrified logs each year.

trails.trailTip: Located right behind the Rainbow Forest Museum, this is a good first stop for seeing the park's largest petrified logs up close.
trails.didYouKnow: 'Old Faithful,' one of the largest logs on this trail, is nearly 10 feet across at its base.

trails.trailTip: Stay on the paved path — removing even small pieces of petrified wood is illegal and has stripped areas near older, unpatrolled trails bare over the decades.
trails.didYouKnow: The 'crystals' in the trail's name are quartz and amethyst that formed inside the logs as they petrified over roughly 200 million years.

trails.bestSeason: Year-round; sunrise or sunset for the best color
trails.trailTip: Time this walk for early morning or late afternoon light, when the badlands' banded colors are most vivid.
trails.didYouKnow: The Painted Desert's banded colors come from iron and manganese minerals deposited in ancient floodplain sediment layers.

trails.trailTip: This loop can be combined with the Agate House spur for a longer walk — carry water, since there's no shade anywhere on the route.
trails.didYouKnow: This area holds one of the densest concentrations of petrified wood in the park, including logs that would have measured over 170 feet long when whole.

trails.trailTip: Agate House is a partially reconstructed pueblo built from petrified wood — stay on the trail and don't climb on the original masonry walls.
trails.didYouKnow: Ancestral Puebloans built this eight-room pueblo almost entirely out of petrified wood roughly 700 years ago.

trails.bestSeason: Oct-Apr; avoid summer heat and afternoon thunderstorms
trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS backcountry-access guidance, this route has no maintained trail and requires a free day-use permit obtained in person at the Painted Desert Visitor Center on the day of your hike, with only a handful issued per week — bring a GPS track, since markers are sporadic and a high-clearance vehicle is needed to reach the start.
trails.didYouKnow: Devil's Playground is known for wind- and water-sculpted hoodoos and a dry waterfall carved into the badlands, with no marked path connecting them.

trails.trailTip: Look for petroglyphs on the boulders near the loop's midpoint, including a solstice marker ancestral Puebloans used to track the sun.
trails.didYouKnow: Puerco Pueblo once housed around 200 people in the 1300s, making it one of the larger villages in the area at the time.

animals.whereToLook: Open grasslands near the Painted Desert and Rainbow Forest areas
animals.viewingTip: View from a road pullout with binoculars — don't approach or chase one for a photo, since pronghorn spook easily and can bolt into traffic.
animals.didYouKnow: Pronghorn are the fastest land animal in North America and can sustain speeds near 55 mph over long distances.

animals.whereToLook: Rocky outcrops along Blue Mesa and Crystal Forest
animals.viewingTip: Observe from a few feet away without cornering it, and use a zoom lens rather than reaching for a closer photo.
animals.didYouKnow: Male collared lizards turn vivid blue-green during breeding season and can run upright on their hind legs when startled.

animals.viewingTip: Watch from the road with binoculars and never feed one — roadside-fed coyotes lose their wariness of vehicles and people, which puts them at greater risk.
animals.didYouKnow: Petrified Forest's coyotes hunt largely by sound, pinpointing rodents moving under grass before pouncing.

animals.viewingTip: Keep food packed away at overlooks and picnic areas — ravens are quick to snatch unattended snacks — and enjoy their acrobatic flight from a distance rather than tossing them food.
animals.didYouKnow: Ravens are among the most intelligent birds studied, capable of solving multi-step puzzles to reach food.

animals.whereToLook: Grassland and badlands habitat, especially near rodent burrows
animals.viewingTip: Admire from a few feet away and let it move on — bullsnakes mimic rattlesnakes by hissing and vibrating their tails when threatened, but are harmless if simply given space rather than handled.
animals.didYouKnow: Bullsnakes are often mistaken for rattlesnakes because of this defensive bluff, but they have no venom and pose no threat to people who leave them alone.

animals.whereToLook: Soaring above the Painted Desert badlands
animals.viewingTip: Scan the sky from overlooks with binoculars; if you notice a nest on a rock ledge, view it from a distance rather than approaching the cliff base.
animals.didYouKnow: Golden eagles can spot a rabbit-sized animal from well over a mile away thanks to eyesight several times sharper than a human's.

animals.whereToLook: Sandy, sparsely vegetated ground in grassland and badlands areas
animals.viewingTip: Look, but don't pick one up — horned lizards rely on staying still and camouflaged, and handling causes real stress; photograph from a low angle instead.
animals.didYouKnow: When seriously threatened, this species can squirt a thin stream of blood from its eyes to deter predators.

animals.whereToLook: Desert grasslands; mostly nocturnal and rarely seen
animals.viewingTip: If you spot a den entrance, observe from well back with binoculars and don't linger nearby — kit foxes will abandon a den if repeatedly disturbed, and food should never be left out to lure one closer.
animals.didYouKnow: Kit foxes are the smallest wild canid in North America, weighing about as much as a housecat.
